source.title: Understanding the double descent curve in Machine Learning
source.authors: Luis Sacouto; J. M. Ramos; Miguel Almeida; A. Wichert

record.tranche_reason: The study reports experiments that reproduce or alter double-descent-like curves and argues that the apparent regime change in neural networks can depend on weight reuse, initialization, and norm constraints.
record.gate_note: The study reports results from model-size sweeps and regularization manipulations. Its discussion of epoch-wise behavior is not an epoch sweep, and it does not vary training-set size. Claims and results cited from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study reruns Belkin et al.'s random-ReLU-feature and weight-reuse neural-network sweeps on MNIST subsets. It then alters the norm bias, L2 strength and weight-reuse switch point, and argues the second descent depends on a low-norm bias. In neural networks it argues the descent is an artifact of the reuse/early-stopping protocol.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that in feature-based models the second descent comes from a bias toward low-norm solutions among infinitely many post-threshold minima. Without that bias the curve follows classical bias-variance. In neural networks the interpolation threshold does not mark a regime change, and the reported descent is an artifact of the weight-reuse/early-stopping protocol. Bias-variance theory remains valid, and over-parameterized models are best when constrained (small init plus early stopping, or weight decay).
record.recipe_differences: The paper reports an exact curve reproduction for a Random ReLU feature-based model and adapts the cited neural-network weight-reuse procedure. It changes the norm constraint, regularization strength, and weight-reuse switch point; it does not test epoch-wise or sample-size double descent.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes change with the norm target, L2 regularization strength, weight-reuse switch point, and early-stopping/initialization conditions.
record.code_released: Code and data available by email request to the first author.
record.problems: The plotted results provide no numerical values or uncertainty estimates in the text. Exact model sizes, regularization settings beyond the stated small lambda, and several dataset details are not stated. The neural-network conclusions are based on the described MNIST subset experiments.

untested.parts: Deep (multi-layer) architectures, width sweeps with standard training from scratch, label noise; no numeric series.
Not tested: no test-error curve over epochs.
Not tested: training-set size not varied.
Only random ReLU features and a one-hidden-layer net; no other model classes (Fourier features, forests, kernels).
Not tested: no effective-complexity measure predicting peak location.
Label-noise dependence, multiple/triple peaks, and optimally tuned regularization are untested; only increasing L2 strength is tested.

record.verdict_notes: All evidence is figure-only, with no numbers, seeds or uncertainty. The neural-network experiments use Belkin's one-hidden-layer protocol, so their bearing on V1 ('deep networks') is limited. Feature-model rows were moved from V1 to V4. Neither original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not provide a numeric error series or a systematic sweep across multiple deep-network architectures.
No test-error curve over training epochs is reported.
Training-set size is not varied to test whether more data raises test error near interpolation.
The experiments cover a Random ReLU feature-based model and neural networks, not a broad survey of model classes.
The study discusses weight norms and model complexity but does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
The study tests changing L2 regularization strength, but not label-noise dependence, multiple or triple peaks, or optimally tuned regularization.
The study does not remeasure complexity using an effective parameter count or show that this turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

relationships.condition: Random ReLU features on a 3000-image MNIST subset, low-norm (R=0) or small-lambda ridge solutions
relationships.reason: Authors report an exact reproduction of the double-descent curve, with good post-threshold test error (r1, r2, r4); figure-only evidence.
relationships.display_finding: Test error reproduced the double-descent curve and improved beyond the interpolation threshold.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Random ReLU features on a 3000-image MNIST subset, low-norm (R=0) or small-lambda ridge solutions
source_check.reason: Figures 6–8 and their accompanying text explicitly report double descent under low-norm or small-lambda fitting.

relationships.condition: Random ReLU features with the ridge penalty pulling toward a point at distance R>0
relationships.reason: With equally valid higher-norm minima the post-threshold regime is worse and there is no second descent (r3). The descent depends on a low-norm tie-breaking bias.
relationships.display_finding: Equally valid higher-norm minima produced worse post-threshold risk and no second descent, making the descent dependent on the preference for low-norm solutions.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Random ReLU features with the ridge penalty pulling toward a point at distance R>0
source_check.reason: The higher-norm experiment shows that post-threshold recovery depends on the solution-selection bias; Figure 7 and its discussion report deterioration instead.

relationships.condition: One-hidden-layer nets on a 4200-image MNIST subset under Belkin's weight-reuse protocol, with reuse continued or the switch point moved
relationships.reason: Without switching off reuse, the threshold has no effect and there is no second descent (r6). The apparent descent tracks the reuse switch point, not the interpolation threshold (r7).
relationships.display_finding: Continuing weight reuse eliminated the second descent; moving the reuse switch moved the apparent descent independently of interpolation.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.condition: One-hidden-layer nets on a 4200-image MNIST subset under Belkin's weight-reuse protocol, with reuse continued or the switch point moved
source_check.reason: The protocol intervention is demonstrated in shallow networks. V1 explicitly concerns deep networks, and the corresponding deep-architecture intervention is untested.

relationships.reason: The second descent past interpolation vanishes without the protocol switch and relocates with it (r6, r7), so here it is not a property of capacity.
relationships.display_finding: The second descent disappeared without the protocol switch and moved when the switch moved.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.reason: Continued reuse eliminates threshold-associated recovery, and changing the initialization switch relocates it, explicitly challenging an intrinsic capacity-threshold interpretation.

relationships.condition: Random ReLU feature regression with increasing L2 penalty
relationships.reason: The overfitting peak disappears and the curve becomes a single descent as lambda grows (r4, r5). This is figure-only, and no optimal lambda is identified.
relationships.display_finding: Increasing λ removed the overfitting peak and produced single descent, without identifying an optimal λ.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Random ReLU feature regression with increasing L2 penalty
source_check.reason: Figure 8's discussion explicitly states that increasing the penalty removes the peak and produces single descent. This supports regularization dependence; optimal tuning, noise dependence and multiple peaks are untested.
